extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent practitioners and applicants (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the §101 subject-matter eligibility analysis (Alice/Mayo framework) including identification of abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature, and application of the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim recites a mental process (abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that can be performed mentally (e.g., by a human using pen and paper) qualify as mental processes and thus may be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have found that claimed steps that can be performed by humans mentally (e.g., listing transactions, computations by pencil and paper) are mental processes (see CyberSource, Flook, Univ. of Florida Research Foundation v. GE, Symantec). Examiners should look to the specification and consider whether claimed steps are performable mentally; if so, treat them as an abstract idea in the eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is claimed as being performed on a computer, it can still recite a mental process (abstract idea) if the underlying concept can be performed purely mentally or is merely the human concept implemented on generic computer resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the specification under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to determine if the invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and the applicant is merely claiming that concept performed: (1) on a generic computer, (2) in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, the claim is considered to recite a mental process (see Benson, Mortgage Grader).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that perform human cognitive actions on generic computer hardware can be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Voter Verified (voting/verifying/submitting votes viewed as human cognitive actions performed on a computer); Versata (determining price using general purpose computer hardware). Even though steps are performed on generic computers, the claims may be 'directed to' abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims describing processes in a computer environment that are analogous to human mental decision-making can be abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Symantec (electronic post office receiving/screening/redistributing mail analogous to human mail decisions); FairWarning (fraud-detection rules are the same questions humans have asked). If with the exception of generic computer-implemented steps there is nothing preventing human performance, treat as mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely use a computer as a tool to perform processes that are mental in nature may be directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping concept performed without a computer); Berkheimer (parsing and comparing data recited at a high level of generality). When steps are at a high level and computers are just tools, the claims may be mental-process abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both product and process claims may recite mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (e.g., computer systems, computer-readable media) as well as process claims can recite mental processes and thus be directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should recognize that claims to systems, media, or methods can all be 'directed to' the same abstract mental concepts. Examples of product claims reciting mental processes include application program interfaces for extracting/processing information, computer systems for anonymous loan shopping, computer-readable media containing fraud-detection instructions, and post-office systems for email (cases: Content Extraction, Mortgage Grader, CyberSource, Symantec, Voter Verified, Electric Power Group, Versata).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract ideas — examiner procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tentative abstract idea' is a claim limitation that an examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas; this requires a defined examiner procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the subject matter eligibility framework: if the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application, the claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If not integrated (Step 2A: YES), proceed to Step 2B: if the claim as a whole provides an inventive concept (Step 2B: YES) it's eligible at Pathway C. If no inventive concept (Step 2B: NO), bring the application to the Technology Center (TC) director — a Step 2B rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director and use form paragraph 7.05.017 with TC Director's signature. The TC Director will notify Patents Management so the public can be informed. Interviews with the examiner are permitted and may advance prosecution; examiner may withdraw or maintain rejections without TC Director interview. Examiner cannot issue a Step 2B rejection for a tentative abstract idea without TC Director approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena — definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or do not have markedly different characteristics compared to nature; courts have labeled them as physical phenomena, scientific principles, natural laws, and products of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions reflect that basic tools of scientific and technological work are not patentable (Funk Bros., Diamond v. Chakrabarty). Examples cited: isolated DNA (Myriad), cloned animals (Roslin), correlations between DNA regions (Genetic Techs.), metabolic correlations (Mayo), myeloperoxidase correlations (Cleveland Clinic), electromagnetism (O'Reilly v. Morse), bacterial qualities (Funk Bros.), primers (Ambry), chemical principles (Tilghman), cell-free fetal DNA (Ariosa), genotype/drug response correlations (Vanda). Examiners should treat claims reciting laws of nature/natural phenomena as judicial exceptions that require further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims describing natural abilities/processes are not automatically laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every claim that describes a natural ability, quality, or process necessarily recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon; eligibility depends on claim focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where claims were eligible: process steps of fractionating, recovering, cryopreserving hepatocytes (Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect) were eligible because they were not focused on merely observing/detecting hepatocyte ability to survive freeze-thaw. Similarly, methods of treating cancer (effect of chemotherapy) or treating headaches with aspirin are not laws of nature. Such claims are eligible at Prong One unless they recite another exception requiring further analysis. Manufacturing processes focused on producing a new compound likewise are not directed to components' abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature — definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, courts may treat it as a 'product of nature' exception; products of nature include naturally occurring products and synthetically created products that lack markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry), cloned animals (Roslin), bacterial mixtures (Funk Bros.). Step 2A uses 'law of nature' and 'natural phenomenon' as inclusive of 'products of nature.' Non-naturally occurring products are not automatically eligible merely because of human intervention; the key is whether they possess markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts (Ambry, Roslin, Chakrabarty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis (purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis identifies whether a nature-based product limitation is a product-of-nature exception by comparing claimed product characteristics to those found in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis is part of Step 2A Prong One. If the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart, the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (NO) at Pathway B unless another exception is present. If it does not have markedly different characteristics, then the claim recites a product of nature and requires further Prong Two analysis (and Step 2B if needed). Case law: Chakrabarty (claimed bacterium had markedly different characteristics and was eligible) and Roslin (claimed sheep lacked markedly different characteristics and was product of nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the analysis only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim; do not overextend it to claim elements that are not nature-based when viewed as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nature-based product can be claimed alone (e.g., 'a Lactobacillus bacterium') or as a limitation within a claim (e.g., a composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk). Examiners should analyze only the nature-based product limitation to determine whether it is a product of nature exception. If the limitation is naturally occurring by its nature, there is no need to perform the analysis because it is directed to a naturally occurring product and falls under the product-of-nature exception by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of markedly different characteristics result
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences for eligibility depending on whether the nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception. For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product, showing a markedly different characteristic means no further analysis is necessary for eligibility (i.e., Step 2B is unnecessary). If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, it recites a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best practices when claim recites a nature-based product with broad BRI
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) encompasses both eligible and ineligible embodiments, examiners should take certain actions to assist prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim recites a nature-based product that, under BRI, may encompass embodiments that lack markedly different characteristics, it is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or that are otherwise eligible. For nature-based product limitations that clearly do not seek to tie up any judicial exception, consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis in MPEP § 2106.06 is appropriate (no need to conduct a markedly different characteristics analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-based product limitations that are naturally occurring — no analysis needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, the markedly different characteristics analysis is unnecessary because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and falls under the product-of-nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should recognize that a claim element that is inherently naturally occurring does not require further markedly different characteristics comparison; it is treated as a product-of-nature exception and proceeds to Prong Two/Step 2B analysis as applicable.
